A variety of connections are used when watching television, talking on the telephone, listening to the radio, or accessing the internet.
Let's look briefly at the variety of links used by a television.
Television signals are sent to the viewer's home, by cable, antenna or satellite. Viewers select the way they receive their signal.

Viewers using cable TV receive their television signals through a coaxial cable. A coaxial cable is a physical link, normally consisting of a single conductor cable. This single conductor carries hundreds of signals simultaneously. This allows the viewer to pick their choice of broadcast at any time..

Viewers using an antenna to receive their television shows pick up signals broadcast through the air. The signal travels from the antenna through a wire to the television. This method of transmission and reception uses physical links (an antenna and wires) and an atmospheric link (air)...

Viewers using a satellite to receive their television shows receive a signal that is first broadcast through the earth's atmosphere to a satellite orbiting earth. The satellite broadcasts are then sent back to earth where they are received by a satellite dish installed at the viewer's home for reception by the television...
Satellite television uses both physical (the satellite, satellite dish) and atmospheric links (air and space).

For example, a voice signal from a telephone travels through wire and, most likely, a fiber optic connection. The wire transfers electrical signals and the fiber optic cable transfers light.
Let's look at some different types of telephone links.
A basic home telephone link is a physical connection link. The link inside the house is usually a four-wire cable (single line telephone only requires a two wire cable).
Fiber Optic Cable with Multiple Conductors and Varying Types
Most often, telephone companies will use fiber optic cables to make connections from their central office to switching offices.

A residence with a computer internet connection will probably use the phone cable; and if the modem is external to the computer, a serial interface cable will be used in addition. It is likely that the signals coming into a home may use other links prior to the connection at the address..

You might be wondering, How does a telecommunications company know which type of link to use? Well, it depends on the type of signal, what type of signal processing needs to take place and how far the signal will be transmitted....

Connection links fall victim to characteristics like, bandwidth restrictions, attenuation losses and EMI (electromagnetic interference). Each one of these is a major consideration when choosing a connection link..

Cables with metallic conductors are used to send and receive information in the form of electricity. There are many varieties in shape and size of metallic conductors (conventional cable). Within a single cable, there can be from one to thousands of conductive elements. Most conductors for metallic cables are made of copper.....

Non-metallic conductors used for fiber optic connections are either glass or plastic. Generally, plastic core cables are used for short distance, lower frequency connection (such as a stereo input), rather than telecommunications...
Fiber Optic Cable with Multiple Conductors and Varying Types
Fiber optic cables are non-metallic cables used to carry information in the form of light. Electrical signals must be transformed into light when being sent by fiber.

Fibers have a number of advantages over metallic conductors.

The practical bandwidth of optical fibers exceeds that of copper cables. A fibers' bandwidth is from 500 GHz to a potential 1 THz (tera or 10 ). All the channels in this bandwidth are far from being used today.y...

Since bandwidth is an effective indication of the rate (bits for digital information) at which information can be sent, and a fiber optic link has a large bandwidth, transmissions of channels requiring much greater bandwidth than a voice is permitted...
For example, the required channel capacity of television and teleconferencing is 14 to 100 times that of digitally encoded voice, making a fiber optic link very desirable for this application.
The bandwidth of the fiber allows these signals to be multiplexed through the fiber. This makes it possible for telephone companies to simultaneously transmit voice, data, and video.

As a signal travels along a transmission path, be it copper or fiber, the signal looses strength. The loss of strength is called attenuation. It is an indication of how far the information can be sent and still maintain the integrity of the transmission....

In a copper cable, attenuation increases with modulation frequency: the higher the frequency of the information signal, the greater is the loss. Loss in coaxial cable and twisted-pair wires increases with frequency..
In an optical fiber, attenuation is flat, meaning the loss is the same at all operating speeds within the fiber's specified bandwidth.
Severe attenuation requires repeaters at intermediate points in the transmission path. A repeater's function is to receive, amplify, and re-transmit the signal.

When comparing copper to fiber, it can be said that copper cable usually requires more repeaters than fiber. This is due to the spacing between repeaters. The spacing between repeaters used with copper cable decreases as operating speeds increase....

Fiber links do not require as many repeaters as copper. This is because, at high data rates very efficient, low-loss fibers are used. This allows repeater spacing to increase with operating speeds....

The combination of high bandwidth and low signal loss has made the telephone industry probably the heaviest user of fiber optics. Not only can more information be sent over a transmission path but also the number of repeaters is decreased. Fewer repeaters means less costly systems...

Fiber links have two safety features that metallic links don't. First, a fiber is not a fire hazard. It does not carry electricity and does not produce a spark, so it cannot cause fires or explosions.
Second, since fiber's are not metal they do not attract lightning. Lightning is attracted to metal, a conductor, therefore metal links are subject to lightning strikes.
These two safety features allow fibers to be installed in areas where the installation and use of metallic cables is hazardous.

When EMI is present you will notice one more of the following; static, noise and/or stray signals. In the case of Digital transmissions, a burst of EMI may appear as an extra pulse in the original pulse stream...

A metallic line's ability to receive and transmit EMI is NOT the only characteristic that makes them un-secure; they are also easy to tap. Tapping a fiber is extremely difficult, and it is virtually impossible to make an undetected tap...

Radio, or wireless telecommunications, has existed for generations. The first wireless telegraph was introduced in 1896. Radio technology has not changed much since then; a radio today still operates on the same principles as the one of yesteryear, propagating frequencies through space....
DISCUSSION
The basic radio system consists of a transmitter, transmitter antenna, receiver antenna and a receiver. The atmosphere provides the link from transmitter antenna to receiver antenna.
The most commonly used radio frequencies (RF) range from

Advancements have come in the form of component construction and modulation techniques. Replacing electron tubes with transistors was a major leap as was the transition from the transistor to the integrated circuit...

Radio problems vary significantly with the modulation method being used. Because there is no way to shield atmospheric connections, interference from severe weather, sunspots, and other naturally occurring phenomena is unavoidable, regardless of the modulation technique applied...

Conversely, radio has an excellent advantage in distance. Some radio connections use the various layers of the atmosphere to bounce (reflect) the transmission to distances they ordinarily could not achieve. Very high frequencies have a tendency to penetrate the earth's atmosphere entirely and travel out into space.....
High-Frequency Radio-Wave (1500-30,00 kHz)
Medium-Frequency Radio-Wave (500-1500 kHz)))

Governmental restrictions apply to radio transmissions with regard to transmitter output power and frequency. Radio remains an efficient and cost-effective way to move information from one place to another...

Microwave is a very broad term used to describe a portion of the frequency spectrum from approximately 1 to 100+ GHz and will be used to describe connections confined to the earth's atmosphere. Airborne and ground-based radar, microwave ovens, and digital cell phones with voice mail, e-mail, caller ID, and two-way paging systems operate in this region.....

The bulk of existing cellular telephony today is analog and falls just short of being considered within the microwave range. However, for the purpose of this lesson, we will categorize all cellular telephony as being microwave in nature...
Microwave data link and repeater stations consist of a transmitter and parabolic antenna as the transmitting station and a receiver and receiving antenna as the receiving station.
Microwaves are ideal for forming data links over long or short paths. Since they have short wavelengths and high gain, parabolic directional antennas are practical.
The transmitting and receiving antennas are high-gain, narrow-beam parabolic antennas. As such, the antennas must be orientated with reference to each other for maximum efficiency.

The output power of a link varies, depending on the bandwidth and, therefore, the number of circuits per carrier, as well as the distance to the next repeater. Powers between .25 and 10 watts are transmitted, with 2 to 5 watts most common...

A microwave link performs the same functions as a copper or fiber-optic cable, but by means of the space wave and therefore limited to line of sight. Many links operate in the 4 to 6 GHz region, but some links operate at frequencies as low as 2 GHz and as high as 13 GHz...

Microwave data links are wideband systems with many channels transmitting simultaneously. With multiplexing techniques, several thousand channels are possible for each carrier frequency that is transmitted to repeater stations spaced 20 to 30 miles apart...

A repeater receives a modulated microwave signal from one transmitter (or repeater) and transmits it to the next one. They are not involved in the modulation process.

An identical chain is provided for working in the other direction. The only difference is that the transmissions in the two directions are somewhat different in frequency to avoid interference. The frequency difference is usually a few hundred megahertz at the 4 or 6 GHz operating frequencies...

Repeater antennas are typically located on towers, hilltops, and skyscrapers so there are no obstructions in the line-of-sight transmission path between two repeater stations. Power requirements at repeater stations are less than a kilowatt...
Since both coaxial media and microwave links are well suited for high-capacity trunks, additional factors must be taken into account when determining the suitability for a given application.

In contrast, coaxial cable is less prone to radio frequency (RF) interference. Microwave radio links rely on the absence of physical as well as electrical obstructions between transmitting and receiving stations. Microwave antenna beam widths can be as narrow as 1 degree..

Trees, buildings, mountains, and even airplanes can interfere with signal transmission. Rain and intense heat can alter the direction of the beam, causing the signal to fade. In large metropolitan areas, microwave beams will often intersect with each other, causing interference...

Microwave links can be used to transmit information short distances, as with police and fire department communication links. They are also used with television microwave links between cities or for transmitting data at much greater distances...

Microwave links are cheaper and have better properties for TV transmission, although coaxial cable is much less prone to interference. The preference is due to the fewer number of repeaters needed for a given distance...

This reduces the cumulative phase and amplitude distortion over the large bandwidth occupied by TV. Microwave links are far more prone to impulse noise than cable, which is protected and a closed-circuit system. Impulse noise is high level, short duration noise that can be caused by electromechanical relays...

An important application of microwave (and UHF) is the RF-based local area network (LAN). The RF-based systems allow signals to penetrate walls, people, or anything that might come between the transmitter and receiver. Infrared systems could also be used, but they are extremely vulnerable to interference...
Microwave radio links are expensive but the costs over coaxial media are offset by these advantages:
4) Shorter distance between switching center
6) Single link, multiple channel transmission

Even though coaxial media and microwave radio links essentially perform the same function, it is not likely that one system will oust the other. The two media are complementary over the backbone routes in most developed countries, although microwave links predominate over the lesser routes...

Satellite communications include television, telephone, global positioning satellites (GPS), secure military communications, and weather information. This link also falls into the microwave range, but it will be distinguished from the microwave category because it involves connections that are outside the earth's atmosphere and propagate in outer space.....

A major advantage of satellites is that they provide services to large numbers of people simultaneously. Hence, point-to-multipoint describes satellite connections, unlike microwave, which is point-to-point. $Back: P3300

The satellite is essentially a microwave relay station placed in orbital space. Telephone and television broadcast signals are beamed up to the satellite from an earth station through the use of a large, highly directive microwave dish antenna that is synchronized to the position of the satellite...
Modern telecommunication satellites are positioned in orbit at an elevation of approximately 22,300 miles above the equator. This is referred to as geosynchronous or geostationary orbit.

At an altitude of 22,300 miles, 40% of the earth is exposed. The satellite's antenna is designed to emit a radiation pattern that covers this entire exposed portion. Satellites positioned in a geosynchronous orbit, 120 degrees apart from each other, can cover the entire surface of the earth, with the exception of the polar caps.....

In this orbit, the satellite is made to travel at a velocity necessary to maintain a fixed position relative to a point above the equator (i.e., it rotates radially with the surface of the earth and therefore remains fixed in the sky 24 hours a day)...

The advantage to geosynchronous orbit is that it permits line-of-sight tracking by earth stations 24 hours a day. Earlier satellites had elliptical orbits and were useful for only short periods of the day...
Other satellites, such as navigational satellites, circle the earth in orbits that are not stationary. Global positioning systems use orbiting satellites.
The range of frequency operation of satellites is from 4 to
30 GHz. Frequency converters are used to convert GHz signals to lower radio frequency signals that can be used by the ground equipment.

A typical satellite system consists of a ground transmission station, a satellite, and the receiving or user station on the ground. The ground transmission station consists of a transmitter and a directional parabolic antenna. Fixed ground stations that transmit to and from a specific satellite can use high-gain, narrow-bandwidth antennas.....
The receiving station consists of a high-gain parabolic antenna, a highly sensitive receiver, and a frequency converter.

Providing strong signal levels to the satellite from the ground station is not a problem. The power for transmission from the ground station is not limited as is the satellite transmitter whose power source is a solar power panel with capabilities limited to about 200 watts..

Since the power source for the satellite is limited, transmitting information over a large surface of the earth reduces the power received to a very small signal level at a particular receiving station. In order for the radiation from the satellite to be received over large areas of the earth's surface, an antenna with a wide beam pattern is required.....
The ground-receiving stations must use very sensitive receivers with high-gain antennas to pick up these signals.
Earth stations typically transmit their signals to satellites on carrier frequencies in the 6 GHz band, ranging from 5.92 to
6.43 GHz. This is called the up-link frequency.

A device called a transponder is used on board the satellite to receive the weak microwave signal, amplify and condition it, and re-transmit the signals back to another earth station in a different location on earth...
The satellite's transponder down-converts these signals to a
4 GHz band, ranging from 3.7 to 4.2 GHz. These frequencies are referred to as the down-link frequencies. Earth station receivers are tuned to these frequencies.

To prevent the transponder's strong transmitted signal from interfering with the earth station's weak received signal, most commercial satellite links separate, transmit, and receive carrier frequencies by about 2 GHz...

Satellite communications are not restricted by topography. Mountains or buildings will not interfere with the receiving antenna's line-of-sight alignment with the satellite, and communications can be maintained. Satellites provide real-time (as it's occurring) intelligence...

Satellites are indispensable to the military because they allow Command and Control centers to make decisions with full knowledge of exact locations of friendly and enemy personnel and armaments. Field commanders receive the same information at the same time, making their tactical situation assessments more precise.....

Maintaining security is difficult when information is sent in a broadcast mode because when a satellite sends information, there's no control over who receives it. Various security measures, such as encryption and burst transmissions, must be taken to safeguard information that is on the airwaves...

Service calls for satellites are particularly expensive and not easily obtained so satellites must be built for extreme reliability. The life expectancy of a satellite is 5 to 10 years, tied directly to the amount of fuel it is designed to carry...

Once a satellite is in orbit and on line, very little is left to do; a dish antenna can be set up at a residence in an hour.
